newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Cho Hung Bank borrows on cheap.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Cho Hung Bank borrows on cheap.

text.p: Cho Hung Bank borrowed on the cheap on Wednesday with a five-year step-up floating rate note.

The US$200 million FRN has a final maturity of five years but can be called at par after three. It pays a coupon of 23 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate for the first three years and LIBOR plus 35.5 basis points thereafter.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was lead manager.
On a blended yield basis, the all-in works out to 31 basis points for five years and 26 basis points for three.
"Thirty-one makes sense for five years," said one banker. But he said investors will assume that Cho Hung Bank will prepay the notes at the call rather than pay the increased coupon.
At 26 basis points for three years, "I would have to say that the deal is still pretty tight because people don't want to accept any less than 29 basis points," he said.
Another syndicate manager said his bank planned to take part in the issue for relationship reasons despite the tight pricing.

Oustanding paper for the top South Korean banks such as A3-rated Cho Hung Bank has been performing well in the secondary market largely on the expectation that the country soon will join the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Neverthless, bankers here have expressed surprise at the pricing levels achieved in some recent issues.
Commercial Bank of Korea, a Baa2 rated bank, managed to get 35 basis points for five years, a spread many bankers in Asia thought was aggressive.
Some said that the issue may have been helped by speculation of a rating upgrade for CBK.
In other news from Asia, Bank of China Hong Kong branch has opted to double its five-year floating rate certificate of deposit issue to HK$4.0 billion, arranger China Development Finance Co said.
The issue totalled HK$2.0 billion at launch but was 4.5 times oversubscribed to HK$9.0 billion. CDFC said 61 banks joined the deal.

Malaysian state oil company Petronas has received an A-plus long-term foreign currency rating on its proposed US$1.0 billion global issue of notes due in 2001 and bonds due in 2006 from Standard and Poor's Corp.
